sentences.text: How about you?
Where are you at?
I'm in Somerset, in England.
Very nice.
Why not?
This meeting is being recorded.
It'll be somewhere.
Right, yeah.
Right, yeah.
Sounds like a nice enough place.
It's lovely.
I have relatives in Bath.
Well, there you go.
They're in Somerset, so.
There you go.
Okay.
Just down the lane.
Which side of the family is it?
Oh, it's my.
My great grandmother moved from there to Oregon in.
Sorry.
My great great grandmother moved to Oregon in the 1890s, so.
Yeah.
Well, I don't know if you know what Bath is like, but it's a beautiful, beautiful city.
It was.
It was built probably just before she moved by the Georgian.
So all the buildings are very, very beautiful.
It's actually a UN Heritage site, so.
Right.
Yeah, yeah, yeah.
I was there once when I was a kid.
I don't really remember.
Everything was just exciting, you know, that.
Hasn'T changed much since this.
Nice.
Yeah.
Well, when it's been preserved, it can't really change, so.
Yeah.
Well, awesome.
Nice to meet you, Andy.
I'll just give you a few details about us.
So we're Capital A.
We're an M and A advisory for marketing services.
So we work both on the buy and the sell side.
We have clients that work with us on Agencies Co, which is our platform for agency buyers and sellers.

And as Capital A is an advisory as well, we work with buyers which tend to either be sort of large growing agencies or agency groups or private equity companies or private investors that are looking to acquire marketing marketing agencies.
So I think in this instance, we have reached out to you because we have a client that's looking to buy in the US actually based in the UK about 95% of our work is with US clients.
But this one just happens to be based in the uk but they are also growing in the US and so they're looking to make some acquisitions.
So they've got more boots on the ground for delivery, so.
So, yeah, so I can get into that.
You can ask some questions about them in a sec.
But it'd be really good to know a little bit more about you guys and where you are at in your journey.
Sure, yeah.
Let's see.
I am.
You know, I definitely wanted to take this call just because this is.
I'm just curious about the process for sure.
And at some point in the next 10 years, I would like to not be the owner of this business.
I'm very involved and I love it.
But also, 10 years is a long.
Normally three years, I hear, but 10, you must have it?
Yeah.
I mean, at some point in the next 10, could be three years, whatever.
So let's see, where are we?
We have been.
Well, I've been doing this work for my whole career, like 26 years.
I started this business six years ago to kind of just go deeper, more specifically to serve the clients that I really wanted to serve, which really are nonprofit organizations.
So the charity folks, that's, that's who we are mostly supporting with their events.
And we do events and some of the other content pieces around the event as well.
But really we assist the client with their planning, their strategy, what's the event for, what are the goals?
And then we go through production, lining up all their vendors and running the thing with them and for them.
And let's see, where are we?
We went through the pandemic.
We actually, it was a wild ride.
We kept working and grew during that time.
We did virtual events and now we're like transition back out into the IRL space and that's where we are 100% now, which is great, actually.
Really great to be back.
Yeah.
So let's see.
And we are, you know, I think in the little that I filled out a little questionnaire, I saw some extra questions.
I mean we are really at half a million dollar a year business.
That's.
And we actually had gone up above that during the virtual event flurry.
But now we seem to be pretty steady between 500 and $600,000 a year.
I don't have like a ton of profits per se because I really try to just make sure that all the folks working with me get paid really well.
So at the end of the year we do a profit share and we pretty much empty the bank account.
So I have, you know, single digit profits to share with everybody.
But that's, that's just our value, the group.
Yeah, yeah.
So I don't know, is that, is that sort of the, the type of, of journey report that you were hoping for?
Anything else?
Yeah, that's pretty good.
So are you an llc?
Is that, are you structured so you.
Yeah, it's an llc.
And we, we report as a S corp for the taxes.
That's cool.
Okay, so it makes sense to just empty the bank account out if you don't need the cash to the team.
All right, brilliant.
So how many people do you have working for you?
Let's see.
Right now I have on our core team four people.
And then we have contractors.
I have a bookkeeper on contract, I have a couple assistants on contract.
I have folks that come in just for event days.
But they're not like on the, on.
The employee team in terms of like what they sort of supply you in terms of skill set.
So what does that team do?
What's the cause things that they are.
I mean, the job title for two of them is event producer.
So they work directly with the client and kind of translate their vision into the event.

So making sure we get the right vendors lined up and that we have the right design and the right vibe and the right entertainment and the right show flow and, and then translating that vision all the way down into really the nitty gritty of ordering supplies and cue sheets and floor plan and rentals.
And there's everything that staffing, you know, everything that's needed to actually create the thing.
So event producers are, they're really like the lead, the lead job.
Got two of those folks and then the other job is production specialist, which is an assistant to that position.
And those folks have, you know, come out of different industries for sure and are just kind of at this point learning, learning their ropes.
But they do some administrative stuff.
You know, they're scheduling meetings, they're sending out agendas and notes, they are updating all of our documents, reaching out to vendors, getting quotes.
You know, it's kind of like running, keeping the engine running on all the projects.
And we do also some, a little bit of graphic design, a little bit of kind of visioning out what, what things are going to look like.
I don't really call us full graphic designers because we don't have that full skill set.
So a bit more like layout and like translating a vision out into.
Out into the space.
Okay.
So it's not just like designing actual sort of things inside the event itself, but it's more outside.
So like you know, invites and web pages or landing pages.
Yeah, we generally.
Well, just because folks usually have a different agency they're working with for that, we generally don't get too involved.
We do sometimes get involved in those like marketing pieces.
Yeah, but it's not our, it's not our core business.
What tends to be your clients?
What do your clients normally look like?
Yeah, they are.
Almost all of them are non profit organizations.
They're mostly looking to throw an event that's a fundraising event just because mostly when nonprofits get together, that's what they want to do is raise some money.
So they are based here in the Seattle area.
Some of them are international NGOs that just happen to be based here.
Others are like working in our community here in Washington state.
Or, or Seattle area.
And they tend to, you know, they tend to have their.
Gosh, it's a pretty big range.
Like, they might have an annual budget of like 5 million up to like, you know, 50 million.
Like, it's.
It's really pretty broad range of type of size of agencies that we work with.
And they're doing events that are like a dinner or sometimes a festival or a concert or, you know, an outdoor event is a.
Yeah.
And usually we're working with them once a year for their signature event.
And then we sometimes have folks that want us to come back and do like a.
More of a suite of events throughout the year.
Right.
Usually once a year, but sometimes more.
And so these NGOs got.
Not great time at the moment with.
Right.
It's.
It's a lot of uncertainty.
Everybody's.
Everybody is that likely to affect your market.
I guess you're.
At least you're in Washington, so you got your own state hidden up in the north.
Correct.
We're our own little nation over here.
We like to think, well, let's see.
So what's interesting, it's good that you're asking that.
I have not had any of my events canceled, like, knock on wood, due to, you know, current worries.
I will say most of our events are the type of event where we are asking individuals and families to step up.
So what's interesting, and this happened for me because I've been doing this for so long in our 2007, 2008 economy crash, that even though, like, a lot of the.
Maybe corporate funding is disappearing and like, other things are really uncertain, that's a time when nonprofits actually go deeper into their individual donors and community.
More fundraising, basically.
Right.
They need to do actually, more fundraising.
So strangely, I.
I feel hopeful that we won't.
You know, the stakes are maybe a little higher because those corporate funders and government grants are not there, but that also makes the urgency higher for the type of work that we do.
So we'll see.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Okay.
So what are you looking for yourself?
So you said you would like to know how this process works.
What's your, your sort of plan over the next, you know, one to ten years?
Yeah, I.

I mean, in my dream, my absolute dream world is that someone who's on my team would want to become the principal and I could just gracefully, like, step to the side and become a senior consultant and then disappear.
That would be ideal.
We've had some of those conversations, and right now I don't see anyone, like, jumping up with that as their goal.
So, yeah, so I don't, I don't currently, you know, I would love for our business to continue because we have a really, you know, really excellent.
Gosh, you know, just like the things we've done and the folks we know and the, the work that we've done over all these years feels really.
It would feel sad to just fold.
Right.
It would feel better to like have Synchronicity continue in some form.

And I think that the fundraising consultancy piece is, you know, I haven't really talked that much about it, but because we are mostly doing this type of, we are offering that strategy and that, that's something very few folks I, in my opinion are doing in a, in a forward looking, innovative way.
So feel super proud of that.
Would hate for it to disappear with me.
So.
So, yeah, I would love for Synchronicity to continue in some way and for me to be able to step down in my work to like working less and working more higher level and less.
Worrying about, can we cover the payroll.
Right, like someone else to worry about that.
So when you say you've got 500k per annum revenue, does that include like the budgets from your clients coming in or is that separate?
Oh, yeah, good question.
No, those are just our fees.
We do not do the work as a general contractor.
We have our clients sign directly with all their vendors.
So those, those fees are really our professional fees.
That so, so that's interesting.
Do you know what you would say the budgets are that you manage?
Oh, yeah.
You know, the absolute minimum event is like 50,000 just to cover like catering venue, basic.
And then some of them are going up to 150,000 per event.
We do about 40 events a year.
So yeah, if we were, if we were doing, if we were running all that money through our bank account, it would be a much larger, much larger enterprise.
So 50k to about 200k for an event.
All right, so your fees are calculated.
How do you take like 10% on whatever the budget is or how do you calculate your fee?
No, we do an estimate on the number of hours that we're going to work on the project for.
Kind of based on, like coming out of the fundraising consultancy world.
It's considered very gauche to take a percentage off of either the budget or the fundraising.
So I just do it really kind of fees for service.
And then, you know, we estimate out.
Sometimes the job becomes a little bigger, so we add some scope, but we keep it pretty simple.
Interesting.
All right, so estimated hours.
So somebody could have a 50k budget, but you will be the same price as somebody that's got a 200k budget.
They just might be more.
Correct.
Yeah, we would be.
I mean, often the people with the bigger budget need more time because they're, they're more difficult like that tends to be.
But they're not, they're not double the difficulty.
They're just like a little more, a little more high touch.
Mm.
All right, so look, just looking at the, the business as it is, so I mean, it's really interesting.
40 events is quite a lot, isn't it?
I mean that's one.
One a week almost all year.
Yeah, yeah.
In, I mean it's interesting in, in pandemic times, we were doing 100 a year because we could stack them, you know, because they're all online.
Right.
But yeah, now that we're back in, in IRL, it's, it's 40 and my team is smaller too, so.
Yeah.
Yeah.

So actually when you look at like your fees because you split them out amongst your team at the end of the year, I mean there's no profit in the business, which is great because you work in the nonprofit space kind of makes.
Makes sense.
But really those are kind of your profits and you split them amongst, amongst your team.
Yeah.
Some agencies do actually report the top number as their revenue, so they would.
Obviously they're still just charging their own fees on it and so their gross margin is exactly what you're reporting at 500k.
But they do say, yeah, we're a 10 million dollar agency.
And actually it's just the cost of.
Putting it just to pass through.
Yeah, no, I don't do that.
Okay, but, but so the way that we work is, is we.

So if we were buying your company on behalf of the client, for instance, we would calculate what your profit margin is and then we would multiply that based on the sort of normal multiples that we see in the marketplace.
So for an events agency under a million, you're probably looking at 4x multiple.
And I guess if you paid everybody what we got, four staff, I don't know, like a going rate, you probably have like 100, 150k left at the end of the year and maybe you cost some money as well.
So maybe there's like 50k left.
So the, the actual company value is possibly something like 200 to 400k at the moment.
Got it.
Which obviously, I don't know, you know, everybody's different, but I don't know if that would get you excited and wanting to sell.

So it perhaps is for you personally to, early in the process where you've, you know, you've only been up and running for six years to sell because you wouldn't, you wouldn't get much out of the other end.

But in terms of like trying to create more value, I think the, the key possibly is to leave that profit in the business because that was, that's going to give you your value each year, even if you take it out as, you know, profits for yourself.
But if you said, you know, my standard salary per year is 150k and I take, you know, an extra 90k in right.
Then at least that 90k would start to give your business a value.
But at the moment be very difficult for you to sell and very difficult for somebody who wanted to acquire to offer you a price.
Right.
Because the, you know, essentially the business isn't worth anything until it's profitable.
I mean, it is in practice it could be, but it just wouldn't be worth very much.
Got it.
Yeah.
So I don't know whether that's just bad news or what you're expecting.
No, that's, that's really interesting.
I, I didn't really have like a, a notion of what I was expecting, so that's actually super helpful.
Yeah, that, that makes a ton of sense.
Yeah.
I mean part of the issue here in the Seattle area is like wages are just super inflated in this area from all of our tech friends who live and work here.
The whole country is, particularly the west Coast.
I mean.
Yeah, it's so, so I feel like that profit share brings our compensation up to a space that at least is not like absurdly low for my team.
So it's, it would be hard to redo that unless I somehow found a way to, to lift up all the fees and you know, but, but I appreciate that, that sort of thinking that through is super helpful.
Yeah.

I mean if I was, if I was going to give you any advice, I would say you might want to look at sort of supplementing maybe even once a quarter like an event where you're working for a for profit company so you could charge more because I think at the end of the day it's going to be your fees.
I guess like you said the word gauche as well.
So just going with that kind of vibe.
I would say because they're non profits, it's probably a bit rude for you to make profit, for you to charge too much because they're seen as charities.

Even though some heads of these companies pay themselves an absolute fortune but you know, so you're kind of stuck with a natural ceiling where it, it becomes a bit crass to start, you know, charging too much.
But what you could supplement that would be to have, you know, a big event for a, for for profit companies and you know, brands, they tend to pay a lot more anyway for events.
So it could be that maybe you just limit yourself to like 10% of the year where you're charging brands and that would help you get more profitable over, over the year.
And then you know it for a small business to have 300, 400, 500k EBITDA or profit margin, it is, it's pretty good, you know, that's pretty good.
And then once you get a multiple of four or five on top of that, the business is worth a couple of mil.
So that's probably where you would want to end up and you'd think, yeah, do you know what?

Somebody is going to give me $1 million to, to work for them for the next two or three years while I run the business into the ground and take all the money out, you know, to run it with, with somebody else who's grow it with you.
At least you'd have cash in the bank and that would be for your worries going forward.
You know, you'll be able to step away, maybe even work on a consultant's basis.
Basis, right?
Yeah, but I would say that's probably the way to go.
Yeah, no, I appreciate it that's any.
Help or whether you, whether I'm being gauche as well, even talking about.
No, I mean you're absolutely.
I appreciate you being sensitive about the fact that there is that ceiling that is in the, is in this space because everyone's just so mindful of their budget.
They just have to be good stewards of, of that, of that budget.
You know, I think because you're in the NGO space, it might be slightly different.

But we, we worked with a client who was a video company and they worked in the same space and not for profits, but generally they had clients that were, well, I would say large corporations that are doing not for profit work.
So their budgets were maybe a little bit bigger.
I think ultimately they were probably doing about 4 or 5 million EBITDA, but we went to market with them.
We found it very difficult to find a buyer just because, for the same reason I think is the, the not for profit space is quite difficult.
It's not like a super competitive space where everybody's trying to buy each other.
So there might not be a huge call for it.
I think the idea of like, maybe trying to find or, or even hire somebody who would make a good leader in the future that could take it off your hands is probably who you need to find.
If you haven't quite hired that person yet, then the next time to find somebody who's really entrepreneurial.
Right, right.
Do you find an odd question, but, like, do you find folks in my situation, like kind of going out with that as part of the conversation?
I just hate to make a promise, like, if it doesn't, you know, end up feeling like a good fit.
Right, yeah.
So it's obviously a tough.
It's a tough one, isn't it?

Because if you sort of christened somebody right at the start like that, you know, sort of king maker, they're always going to be difficult with all the other staff and it could, it might not turn out well.
Anyway, like you say, you might end up having to fire them, so it might not be the best situation.
What we find is just very generally talking to employees about selling just gets everybody nervous.
So it's not the best thing to talk to.
You don't realize as an entrepreneur yourself is that you are an exceptional person.
You're like a 1% of the population just before you've even got out of bed.
And so finding that 1% amongst, you know, the people that you may speak to is going to be.
Is going to be tough.
So.
Yeah, I think you just need to look for entrepreneurs that can take the responsibility over time and not mention it, but.
Right.
They start to develop a sort of sense of responsibility for certain aspects of the business.
Then they would obviously be the best candidates.
Got it.
Doing a, a management buyout as, as it's known in the trade, an mbo, where the management buy the company and take.
All right, well, thank you, Andy.
Appreciate all your, all your good notions here.
I don't know whether I've been any help or whether I've just gone.
No, I mean, I can tell you're in, in this work and you understand it very well.
So I appreciate the free consulting and.
Yeah, no, my pleasure.
Well, you know, I can't make off, you know, you make me feel bad.
Oh, no, I'm joking.
I'm joking.
But like I said, we've worked in this space before.
I know it's a tough.
I know it's tough space.
Yeah, it's, it's tough.
But, you know, clearly you're doing really good work.
I love your dresses, by the way.
What, what are you looking at?
That they.
Our process page.
You've got, like.
Oh, good.
Oh, yeah, that's someone else.
I can tell you've got a style for the pinched shoulders, but my wife really likes those types of dresses as well.
Oh, nice.
Yeah, that's right.
This look awesome.
Well, enjoy yourself there in Somerset.
And it was nice to meet you.
I will.
Getting dark outside.
All right, see you later.
Enjoy the rest of your day.
Bye.

summary.action_items:
**Alex Martin**
Consider supplementing nonprofit events with for-profit company events to increase profitability (17:58)
Look for entrepreneurial employees who could potentially take over the business in the future (22:50)
summary.overview: In the Exploratory Business Consultation meeting between Alex Martin and Andy Day, the discussion centered on Alex's event production business, which specializes in servicing nonprofit organizations primarily in the Seattle area. With an annual revenue between $500,000-$600,000 and a focus on signature events, the business has a core team of four and operates around 40 events per year, managing budgets from $50,000 to $150,000. Alex expressed a desire to exit the business within the next decade, while Andy provided strategic advice on enhancing the company’s valuation through profit retention and exploring additional revenue streams by incorporating for-profit events. The meeting concluded with action items for Alex to seek entrepreneurial employees for future succession and to diversify his event offerings to bolster profitability.
summary.short_summary: In a meeting between Alex Martin and Andy Day, Alex shared insights about his event production business that focuses on nonprofit organizations in Seattle, generating annual revenues of $500,000 to $600,000. With a core team of four and around 40 events annually, Alex aims to exit the business in the next ten years. Andy provided strategic advice on increasing the company's valuation by retaining profits and diversifying revenue streams through for-profit events. Additionally, they discussed the current team structure, client demographics, and budget ranges for events, emphasizing the need for entrepreneurial employees to facilitate succession planning. The meeting concluded with action items for Alex to explore new event offerings to enhance profitability and ensure a smooth transition in leadership.
